chapters.title: Descent into the Maelstrom
chapters.passage:
I read about the Maelstrom in a book and I always wanted to see it. The Maelstrom appears in the sea near the coast of Norway.

In the northwest of that country there is a region called Nordland. And near the coast of Nordland, there is a group of islands called Lofoten. Two of the Lofoten Islands are called Moskoe and Vurrgh. Between Moskoe and Vurrgh, there is a narrow place where the sea turns and races in a great circle. This is the Maelstrom-a whirlpool.

In the Maelstrom, the sea rises up and then falls. As the sea falls, it turns in a circle. It turns faster and faster. It is the same as water going down into a huge pipe. The Maelstrom is very dangerous for boats and ships. It pulls them down into the sea. Many ships have sunk and many men have died in the dangerous water.

I wanted to see the great whirlpool, so I went to Norway. When I got to Nordland, I found a guide. I paid this man to show me the Maelstrom. He took me to the top of a cliff early one morning.

"This is the best time to see the whirlpool," he said.

We came to the edge of the cliff and looked down. The sea was more than a thousand feet below us.

I stepped back from the edge quickly. I felt ill and afraid. I wanted to sit down. The wind was blowing very strongly and the waves of the sea crashed against the rocks below us. I thought that I was going to fall over the edge of the cliff.

"We are on the side of a mountain called Helseggen the Cloudy," said my guide. He reached out his hand and pointed across the sea toward a group of islands. "Look, those are the Lofoten. Can you see the two smallest islands? They are Moskoe and Vurrgh. No one lives there. Now listen and look at the sea between the islands."

I looked at the two smallest islands. They were black rocks. No one could live on them. I listened and heard the sound of the wind. But then I heard another sound. It was a low sound. It sounded like hundreds of huge animals were calling and running together. I could hear the sound and I could feel the sound. I could feel the low sound in my body.

"The tide is turning," said my guide. He pointed down to the sea below us. "The tide turns twice each day. Look at the sea! It is turning and moving in another direction!"

I looked to where the man was pointing. The dark water far below us was as black as oil. I watched it moving slowly. It started to rise and turn, as if it were a pot of hot water on a fire. But the seawater was not hot; it was as cold as ice. The wind blew the tops of the waves. It made many tiny bubbles of air in the water. The tiny bubbles became white foam. Soon, more and more white foam appeared on the black sea. My guide pointed toward the islands of Moskoe and Vurrgh again.

"Watch the sea between the islands!" he shouted.

Then there was another change in the sea. The water became smoother, but it did not become calmer. The dark water started to move in a huge circle. It moved very quickly. It spun around and around. The edge of the circle was white with foam. It was amazing.

"Is-is that the great whirlpool? The Maelstrom?" I asked.

"Yes," said my guide, "that is the terrible Maelstrom. When fishermen sail toward this coast, they look for Moskoe. They do not come closer than a mile."

"Do fishermen sail near these islands?" I asked. I could not believe this.

"Yes, they do. I did. I was a fisherman once. There are a great many fish near Moskoe."

"But isn't it too dangerous to fish here?" I asked.

"Fishermen know when the tides rise and fall. There are two times in the day when it is safe. We go out when the sea is calm and smooth. Then we come back twelve hours later."

"And is fishing always safe at those times? Are boats and ships never lost?" I asked.

"Many boats and ships are lost in the Maelstrom," the man said. "Fishermen make mistakes and their boats are pulled down. Sometimes larger ships are lost in the Maelstrom when they come too close. The sea is calm one moment, and a storm can be blowing five minutes later."

I looked at the Maelstrom in amazement. I could not believe it! The whirlpool was moving faster and faster. As the whirlpool moved, the water in its center dropped down. There was now a hole, or pit, in the center of the whirlpool!

"Nothing can go into that hole and come out alive," I said. "It is a huge, round mouth in the sea. That mouth will swallow everything that comes near it. It makes me afraid."

"That is true," said my guide. "The Maelstrom swallows ships and whales and men. But one man went into the Maelstrom and came out alive."

"Surely, that is impossible!" I said.

I looked at the round, black mouth in the sea. My body shook with fear. The white foam made me think of teeth. Terrible teeth. And the noise of the wind and water! It was the noise of a monster eating rocks.

"How old do you think that I am?" asked my guide. He shouted these words. I shook my head. It was difficult to hear his voice. The noise of the Maelstrom was now very loud. We moved back from the edge of the cliff. We went and sat behind some rocks.

"How old do you think that I am?" the man asked again.

I did not understand the reason for his question. His hair was white and he had many lines on his face. He moved slowly. He must be an old man.

"Are you more than sixty years old?" I asked.

"No. I am forty," said my guide. "The Maelstrom made me old. I'll tell you my story. It happened three years ago."

This is my guide's story. I am writing his words.

One day in the summer, my brothers and I went out in our fishing boat. It was seven o'clock in the morning of July 10th. The sea was calm and smooth. We sailed past Moskoe Island to look for fish.

There were many fish in the sea that day. We caught a large number of them and loaded them into our boat. We were very busy and we forgot how many hours had passed.

In summer, we have nearly twenty hours of daylight in Norway. The nights are short. There are only four hours of darkness. When I looked at my watch, I saw that it was six o'clock in the evening.

We had to pass Moskoe Island at seven o'clock. That was the time when the tide turned. It was safe at seven o'clock that day. We were about an hour away from Moskoe. We started to return home immediately.

A storm came suddenly. Dark clouds covered the sky and the wind started to blow. Our boat raced before the storm. Faster and faster, we sailed toward home and safety.

When I looked to the northeast, I saw Moskoe Island. The sea was moving very quickly, but it was almost the safe time of the day. It was almost seven o'clock. I was sure of this. I took my watch out of my pocket again and looked at it. Then I had a terrible shock. My watch still showed six o'clock. It had stopped!

My brothers were in the front of the boat. I called to them.

"The Maelstrom!" I shouted. "My watch was wrong! We are too late!"

It was not the safe time of day. It was the time when the great whirlpool opened like a mouth in the sea. We were going to die!

Our boat shook. It shook as if it were a dog throwing water off its body. Then the boat suddenly became still.

A few seconds later, the tide picked up our boat and started turning it. It pulled us into the circle of white water around the edge of the whirlpool.

Our boat moved slowly and steadily around the edge of the whirlpool. It circled many times. Each time that our boat circled, it moved a little closer to the great mouth in the sea. From the edge of the circle, the wall of the pit was as steep as a cliff. I had to look down at it. I could not turn my head away.

Around and around we went. My brothers held onto the mast in the center of the boat. We could not speak. The noise of the wind and water was too loud.

I could not hold onto the mast. I held onto a wooden barrel. It was our barrel of drinking water. The barrel was almost empty.

Our boat moved faster and faster. Now, the clouds had disappeared from the sky and we saw the moon.

I thought that we had been in the whirlpool for many hours. The hours of darkness are between two and seven o'clock in the morning. Could we live a little longer? The safe time of the day was seven o'clock. Could we live for three, or maybe four hours more?

The answer was no. The moon showed us the black mouth in the sea. We were going to fall into that mouth.

But we did not fall. The boat did not fall suddenly from the wall of water. We moved down smoothly and steadily.

I had time to think about death-my death. I thought about the water going into my mouth and lungs. I was going to drown. Was the sea going to take our bodies and keep them? Or was it going to throw our bodies back onto the land?

I looked down into the black pit. Our boat was on the side of the wall of water. The wall of water was turning faster and faster. I looked straight down the pipe of water but I did not fall. We were moving so quickly in a circle, that we did not fall. I was amazed.

The air raced past me. I was on the edge of death, but I was alive. It was strange. I was excited.

But the fear of death fell on my brothers. They took a rope and tied themselves to the mast in the center of the boat. I also took a piece of rope. I tied the rope around my body and onto the barrel.

Where was the bottom of the sea? It could not be far. And I knew that there were sharp rocks at the bottom of the sea. We were going to be cut and broken on the rocks!

Our boat moved lower and lower down the black pipe-Then the boat moved to the left and the right. It shook. I was thrown into the black water of the pit. But I did not sink beneath the water because I was tied to the barrel. The barrel stayed on the top of the water.

I saw the boat and my brothers fall down into the pit. We were turning around in the whirlpool. Then the boat disappeared and I started to rise. The barrel moved up slowly. And it took me with it.

Then, suddenly, I was no longer in danger. One moment, I was on the wall of water. The next moment, I was on the top of flat, smooth water. The sea had changed. It was calm. The whirlpool had disappeared. I was no longer looking down. I was looking up. I was looking up at the sky.

It was dawn and the sun was shining. Sunlight shone from behind the mountain, Helseggen the Cloudy. Fishermen were sailing their boats toward me. They pulled me from the water.

No one believed my story. My brothers never returned. Our boat never returned. And my friends and family did not know me. I now looked twenty years older. My black hair had become white. Fear had made lines on my face.

questions.question: Main Idea: What is the main focus of this story?
options: An explanation of the geography and tides of the Lofoten Islands in Norway.
A man's terrifying, first-hand account of surviving a deadly whirlpool called the Maelstrom.
A guide teaching a tourist how to become a successful fisherman in Nordland.
questions.explanation: While the story begins with a description of the location, the core narrative is the guide's incredible flashback of surviving the whirlpool.

questions.question: Detail: Where exactly is the Maelstrom located?
options: In a narrow passage between the islands of Moskoe and Vurrgh off the coast of Nordland.
At the very top of a mountain called Helseggen the Cloudy.
In the center of the capital city of Norway.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states it is located between the two smallest Lofoten Islands, Moskoe and Vurrgh, off the coast of Nordland.

questions.question: Inference: When the narrator first looks down at the Maelstrom from the cliff, he steps back quickly, feels ill, and wants to sit down. What does this reaction suggest?
options: He has a severe fear of heights.
The sheer power, height, and noise of the sea below completely overwhelm and terrify him.
The guide pushed him toward the edge.
questions.explanation: The sensory overload of looking down a thousand feet at the violently turning black water and hearing the deafening roar makes him physically ill and terrified of falling.

questions.question: Detail: The guide explains that fishermen still go near the dangerous islands. How do they avoid the whirlpool?
options: They use large, heavy ships that the whirlpool cannot pull down.
They only fish at two specific times of the day when the tide changes and the sea is temporarily calm.
They always fish from the shore and never use boats.
questions.explanation: The guide explains they use their knowledge of the tides to go out only during the two brief, twelve-hour intervals when the sea is smooth.

questions.question: Text Structure: How is the narrative structured?
options: It begins with a present-day observation of the whirlpool, followed by the guide's flashback story of his survival.
It follows a chronological timeline starting from the guide's childhood.
It alternates between the perspectives of the guide and his two brothers during the storm.
questions.explanation: The framing device introduces the tourist and the guide in the present, which seamlessly transitions into the guide narrating his past trauma.

questions.question: Inference: When the narrator looks at the Maelstrom, he says the white foam makes him think of "terrible teeth" and the noise sounds like "a monster eating rocks." What literary device is the author using?
options: Personification/Metaphor, comparing the inanimate whirlpool to a living, hungry, destructive beast.
Foreshadowing that they will discover a real sea monster at the bottom.
Irony, because the whirlpool is actually very safe.
questions.explanation: The author is using vivid figurative language to compare the deadly natural force of the Maelstrom to a terrifying, destructive creature.

questions.question: Detail: Why does the narrator mistakenly assume his guide is over sixty years old?
options: Because the guide tells him he has been fishing for sixty years.
Because the guide has white hair, deep lines on his face, and moves slowly, despite only being forty.
Because the guide is the narrator's grandfather.
questions.explanation: The intense fear from his ordeal aged him prematurely, turning his hair white and lining his face, making a forty-year-old look over sixty.

questions.question: Detail: On the day of the disaster, why didn't the guide and his brothers return to safety before the Maelstrom formed?
options: They decided to stay and catch more fish because the weather was so perfect.
They fell asleep in the boat because they had been working for twenty hours.
The guide's watch had broken and stopped at six o'clock, making them think they had an hour left before the dangerous tide turned at seven.
questions.explanation: They lost track of time catching fish, and when the guide checked his watch, it falsely read six o'clock, tricking them into thinking they had time to beat the seven o'clock tide change.

questions.question: Inference: The guide says his boat "shook as if it were a dog throwing water off its body" before being pulled into the whirlpool. What does this suggest about the boat's situation?
options: The boat was fighting against the extreme, chaotic forces of the sudden storm and the turning tide.
There was an actual dog on the boat that was scared.
The boat had completely sunk at that exact moment.
questions.explanation: This simile vividly describes the violent, shuddering impact of the conflicting currents and storm winds hitting the small vessel.

questions.question: Detail: While circling the whirlpool, what object does the guide hold onto instead of the mast?
options: A piece of broken sharp rock.
A nearly empty wooden barrel used for drinking water.
A rope that belonged to his brother.
questions.explanation: The text clearly notes his brothers took the mast, so he held onto their nearly empty wooden drinking water barrel.

questions.question: Inference: The guide says, "I looked straight down the pipe of water but I did not fall. We were moving so quickly in a circle, that we did not fall." What physical principle is keeping the boat on the wall of water?
options: Centrifugal force generated by the extreme speed of the spinning water pushes them against the wall.
The boat was equipped with a special engine that pushed it upward.
The moon's gravity was pulling the boat out of the water.
questions.explanation: The extreme velocity of the spinning water creates a centrifugal effect, pressing the boat outward against the steep, vertical wall of the whirlpool, preventing an immediate free-fall.

questions.question: Inference: While facing imminent death in the pit, the guide says, "I was on the edge of death, but I was alive. It was strange. I was excited." What is a likely explanation for this feeling?
options: He was happy that he was finally going to drown.
The sheer, unbelievable spectacle of the massive natural phenomenon briefly overrode his terror with a sense of awe and adrenaline.
He knew the fishermen were already coming to save him.
questions.explanation: Facing the absolute certainty of death, his mind shifts from panic to a morbid, adrenaline-fueled fascination with the incredible power of the vortex around him.

questions.question: Detail: How does the guide ultimately survive while his brothers do not?
options: He ties himself to the wooden water barrel, which keeps him afloat when he is thrown into the water, while his brothers go down with the heavy boat.
He unties his brothers and pushes them into the water so he can take the mast.
He climbs the wall of water using a rope.
questions.explanation: By lashing himself to the buoyant barrel, he stays near the surface when the boat is violently tossed, allowing him to rise while the boat and mast drag his brothers down.

questions.question: Detail: What happens when the safe time of day arrives?
options: The whirlpool suddenly reverses direction and shoots him onto the beach.
The sea becomes calm and flat, the whirlpool disappears, and nearby fishermen pull him from the water.
A giant whale swallows him and carries him to Moskoe Island.
questions.explanation: As the tide changes, the vortex collapses, leaving the sea flat and calm, allowing the morning fishermen to easily rescue him.

questions.question: Purpose: Why does the author end the story by stating that the guide's friends and family did not recognize him?
options: To emphasize the profound, permanent physical and psychological toll the horrifying experience took on him.
To explain why the guide decided to move away from Norway.
To show that his family was angry with him for losing the fishing boat.
questions.explanation: The fact that his own family didn't recognize him serves as a haunting conclusion, proving how the extreme terror fundamentally destroyed his youth and appearance.

chapters.title: The Signalman
chapters.passage:
'Hello!'

When I called the signalman, I was above him on the hill. But he did not look up. He looked along the railway line towards the tunnel.

'Hello, down there!' I called again.

Then he looked up and saw me.

'Where's the path?' I asked. 'How can I come down and speak to you?'

He did not answer me. Just then a train came out of the tunnel. The signalman had a flag in his hand and he showed it when the train passed. Again I asked him where the path was. He pointed his flag at the hill, and I saw a path that went down.

'Alright! Thanks!' I shouted.

I went down the wet path. The signalman was waiting for me at the bottom of the hill. He was standing between the railway lines with a strange, nervous expression on his face.

The place was quiet and lonely. High walls blocked out a lot of the sky, so there was not much sun there, and it was dark. I looked along the line and saw a red light in front of the entrance to the black tunnel. Then I went up to the signalman, but he moved away from me. He looked at me strangely.

'It's very lonely here,' I said. 'You don't get many visitors. Am I disturbing you?'

He did not answer, but looked at the red light near the tunnel.

'Why are you watching that light?' I asked. 'Is that part of your job?'

He answered quietly, 'Don't you know it is?'

Suddenly the horrible idea came to me that he was a ghost, not a man. So I moved away. But then I saw fear in his eyes.

'Are you afraid of me?' I asked.

'I was thinking perhaps I've seen you before.'

'Where?'

He pointed to the red light. 'There.'

'Why? I've never been there before.'

'No, perhaps you haven't.'

Then he began to relax. He took me into his signal box.

'Have you got much work to do here?' I asked.

'No, not very much. But I have to be very attentive and careful,' he replied.

'What are your responsibilities?'

'I change the signal, pull these switches, and check that the red light is working,' he explained.

'Do you ever feel lonely?' I asked.

'No, I'm used to it.'

'Can't you ever go out into the sunlight?'

'Yes, sometimes when the weather is good. But I must always listen for the electric bell and watch the red light.'

I looked around his signal box. There was a fire, a desk, a telegraph machine for receiving and sending messages and a little electric bell.

'When I was a young man, I studied science,' he told me.

The bell suddenly rang. He received messages and sent replies. Then he showed his flag when a train passed. He did everything very precisely. During our conversation he opened the door twice and looked at the red light. He came back to the fire with an anxious expression. I wanted to know why, so I asked, 'Are you a happy man?'

'I was happy once,' he replied. 'But now I'm worried, sir.'

'Why? What's the problem?'

'It's difficult to say. If you come again, I'll try and tell you,' he said.

'When shall I come?'

'I'll be here again at ten o'clock tomorrow night, sir.'

'I'll come at eleven then,' I replied.

It was dark outside, so he showed me to the path with his light.

'Don't call out "hello" again, please,' he said.

'Alright.'

'And don't call out when you come tomorrow night. Why did you shout "Hello, down there!" tonight?' he asked.

'I don't know. Did I say those exact words?'

'Yes. I know those words very well.'

'I think I said them because I saw you down here,' I said.

'Is that the only reason?'

'Yes, of course. Why?'

'You don't think there was any supernatural reason?' he asked.

'No.'

Then we said goodnight, and I returned to my hotel.

I arrived at eleven the following night. The signalman was waiting for me with his light. 'You see, I didn't call out,' I said, smiling. We walked to the signal box and sat down by the fire.

'I've decided to tell you what disturbs me,' he began in a quiet voice. 'Yesterday evening I thought you were somebody else.'

'Who?' I asked.

'I don't know.'

'Does he look like me?'

'I've never seen his face because his left arm is always in front of it. He waves his right arm - like this.' And he waved violently, like somebody trying to say, 'Please get out of the way!'

'One night,' continued the signalman, 'the moon was shining and I was sitting here. Suddenly I heard a voice - "Hello, down there!" I went to the door and looked out. There was somebody by the red light near the tunnel and he was waving. "Look out! Look out!" he shouted, and then again, "Hello, down there! Look out!" I took my lamp and ran towards him. "What's wrong? What's happened?" I called. I wondered why he had his arm in front of his eyes. As I came near him, I put out my hand to pull his arm away - but he wasn't there.'

'Did he go into the tunnel?' I asked.

'No. I ran into the tunnel. I stopped and shone my lamp around, but there was nobody there. I was scared, so I ran out fast and came to my box. I sent a telegraph message "Alarm received. Is anything wrong?" The answer came back: "All well."'

I said that the person was probably a hallucination.

'Wait a moment, sir,' the signalman said, touching my arm. 'Six hours later a terrible accident happened on this line. They brought a lot of dead and injured people out of the tunnel.'

'But it was only a coincidence,' I said. 'A very strange coincidence.'

'Excuse me, but I haven't finished yet, sir.'

'I'm sorry,' I replied.

'This was a year ago. Six or seven months passed and I recovered from the shock. Then one morning at dawn I saw the ghost again.'

'Did it call out?' I asked.

'No. It was silent.'

'Did it wave its arm?'

'No. It had its hands in front of its face like this.' He covered his face with his hands.

'Did you go up to it?'

'No. I came in and sat down, very frightened,' he said. 'When I went back to the door, the ghost was gone.'

'And afterwards? Did anything happen this time?' I asked again.

'Yes. That day a train came out of the tunnel, and I saw in a carriage window a lot of people standing up looking agitated. I gave a signal to the driver to stop. When the train stopped, I ran to it and heard terrible screams. A beautiful young lady was dying in one of the carriages. They brought her here and put her down on the floor between us.'

I pushed back my chair in horror.

'It's true, sir. That's exactly what happened. Now listen and you'll understand why I'm worried. The ghost came back a week ago, and I've seen it again two or three times.'

'Is it always at the red light?' I asked.

'Yes, the danger light.'

'What does it do?'

'It waves like this,' he replied. He repeated the movements that expressed the words "Please get out of the way!" Then he continued. 'I have no peace or rest. It calls me many times - "Hello, down there! Look out!" And it rings my bell.'

'Did it ring your bell yesterday when I was here?' I asked him.

'Twice,' he replied.

'Oh, it's your imagination! I was looking at the bell and listening for it, but it only rang when the station called you.'

The signalman shook his head. 'No, the ghost's ring is different. You didn't see or hear it - but I did.'

'And was the ghost there when you looked out?'

'Yes, twice.'

'Will you come to the door with me and look for it now?'

He came to the door and I opened it.

'Can you see it?' I asked.

'No. It's not there.'

'Right,' I said.

We went in, shut the door and sat down. Now I was certain that the ghost did not exist.

'I think you understand,' he said, 'that I'm disturbed by one question: what does the ghost mean?'

'No, I don't understand you.'

'What is the ghost warning me about? What is the danger? Where is it? Some horrible disaster is going to happen, but what can I do? I can't send a telegraph to the station. What can I say? Message: "Danger! Take care!" Answer: "What danger? Where?" Message: "Don't know. But be careful!" They'll think I'm mad.'

The poor signalman looked very worried. He pushed his fingers into his black hair. Then he took his handkerchief and wiped his face and hands.

'Why doesn't the ghost tell me where the accident will happen? Why doesn't it tell me how I can prevent it? Why didn't it say that the beautiful young lady was in danger? My God, I'm only a poor signalman! Why me!'

I tried to calm him down. I said he must do his duty well, as correctly as possible - and that was all. He became calm after a while, and I offered to stay with him for the night.

'No, it's alright, thank you,' he said. 'Come back an hour after sunset tomorrow.'

I left him at two o'clock in the morning. In my hotel room I thought about what to do. The signalman was intelligent, careful and correct in his work. But the situation disturbed him very much. How could he continue to do his job well? So I finally decided to take him to the best doctor in town.

The next evening I went out early. It was nearly sunset when I reached the path above the railway. I had another hour before the signalman came, so I decided to go for a walk. But as I looked down at the railway I saw a man at the tunnel. He had his left arm in front of his eyes, and he was waving violently.

I cannot describe my horror. But it passed when I saw that the man was not a ghost. He was a real person, and there were some other men not far away from him. The red light was not shining. Near it was a small object like a bed covered with a sheet. I ran down the path very fast.

'What's the matter?' I asked the men.

'The signalman is dead, sir,' one of them said.

'What? The man I know?'

'If you know him, you'll recognise him.' And the man pulled back the sheet.

'Oh, how did this happen?' I cried, recognising the dead signalman.

The man at the tunnel came forward and spoke. 'A train knocked him down and killed him this morning. It was just getting light. The train came out of the tunnel, and he was standing with his lamp near the line, with his back to the train. Show the gentleman, Tom.'

'I'm the train driver, sir,' Tom said. 'I saw the signalman as I came towards the end of the tunnel. There was no time to slow down. He didn't hear my whistle, so I shouted very loudly.'

'What did you say?'

'I said, "Hello, down there! Look out! Look out! Please get out of the way!" I called to him many times, and I put this arm in front of my eyes because I didn't want to see, and I waved this arm like this but it was too late...'

questions.question: Main Idea: What is this story mostly about?
options: A train driver who accidentally hits people on the railway.
A signalman who receives supernatural warnings before terrible accidents happen.
A man who gets lost on a hill and makes a new friend.
questions.explanation: The entire plot revolves around the signalman's terrifying experiences with a ghostly figure that appears just before fatal accidents occur on his railway line.

questions.question: Detail: When the narrator first calls out "Hello, down there!", what does the signalman do?
options: He immediately runs up the hill to meet the narrator.
He ignores the narrator, looking along the railway line towards the tunnel instead.
He throws his flag on the ground.
questions.explanation: The text states that when the narrator first called, the signalman did not look up but looked along the railway line towards the tunnel.

questions.question: Inference: When the narrator first meets the signalman, the narrator thinks he might be a ghost. Why?
options: Because the signalman is transparent and floating.
Because the signalman acts very strangely and asks if the narrator is the ghost instead.
Because the signalman lives in a very lonely, dark place and looks at him with a strange, nervous expression.
questions.explanation: The narrator notes the place is quiet, lonely, and dark, and when the signalman moves away and looks at him strangely, the narrator gets the "horrible idea" that he is a ghost.

questions.question: Detail: What are the signalman's main job responsibilities?
options: He sells tickets to passengers and cleans the tunnel.
He changes the signal, pulls the switches, and checks that the red light is working.
He drives the trains back and forth through the tunnel.
questions.explanation: When asked about his responsibilities, the signalman explicitly says, "I change the signal, pull these switches, and check that the red light is working."

questions.question: Detail: What happened six hours after the signalman saw the ghost for the first time?
options: A terrible accident happened on the line, and dead and injured people were brought out of the tunnel.
The signalman fell asleep and missed a telegraph message.
A beautiful young lady died in a train carriage.
questions.explanation: The signalman explains that six hours after seeing the ghost and sending an alarm, a terrible accident happened and dead and injured people were brought out of the tunnel.

questions.question: Inference: Why was the signalman so afraid when the narrator first yelled "Hello, down there!"?
options: Because the signalman does not like visitors.
Because those were the exact same words the ghost shouted before the first terrible accident.
Because he thought the narrator was a train driver.
questions.explanation: The signalman is frightened and asks the narrator why he used those exact words, stating, "I know those words very well," because they are the same words the ghost used.

questions.question: Detail: What was the ghost doing the second time the signalman saw it?
options: It was waving a red flag violently.
It was ringing the electric bell very loudly.
It was silent and had its hands in front of its face.
questions.explanation: The signalman tells the narrator that during the second appearance, the ghost did not call out or wave, but "It was silent" and "had its hands in front of its face."

questions.question: Inference: After the ghost appeared the second time, a young lady died on a train. What pattern is the signalman noticing?
options: That the ghost always appears right before a terrible tragedy happens on the railway.
That the ghost only appears to women.
That the ghost wants him to quit his job.
questions.explanation: The signalman realizes that the ghost is a supernatural warning sign; each time he sees it, a horrific, fatal event follows shortly after on his railway line.

questions.question: Detail: Why does the signalman feel helpless when he sees the ghost for the third time?
options: Because he does not know how to use the telegraph machine.
Because he knows a disaster is coming, but the ghost doesn't tell him what the danger is or how to prevent it.
Because the narrator refuses to help him.
questions.explanation: The signalman is highly distressed because he receives the warning but doesn't know what to tell the station; if he sends a vague message about an unknown danger, "They'll think I'm mad."

questions.question: Inference: The narrator watches the electric bell, but doesn't hear it ring when the signalman says the ghost is ringing it. What does the narrator believe?
options: The narrator believes the bell is broken.
The narrator believes the ghost is invisible to everyone except the signalman.
The narrator believes the signalman is imagining things and the ghost does not exist.
questions.explanation: After they check outside and see nothing, and after the narrator fails to hear the ghost's bell ring, the narrator states, "Now I was certain that the ghost did not exist."

questions.question: Detail: What does the narrator decide to do to help the signalman the next day?
options: He decides to take the signalman to the best doctor in town.
He decides to report the signalman to the railway station.
He decides to bring him a new red light.
questions.explanation: The narrator feels the situation disturbs the signalman too much for him to do his job well, so he decides to take him to the best doctor in town.

questions.question: Text Structure: How does the author build suspense at the end of the story?
options: By having the narrator find the signalman sleeping on the job.
By showing the narrator a man waving his arms exactly like the ghost, only to reveal it is a real tragedy.
By describing a long walk through the forest.
questions.explanation: The author creates tension when the narrator arrives and sees a figure waving just like the ghost, which initially causes horror until the narrator realizes it's a real person standing over the dead signalman.

questions.question: Detail: How did the signalman die?
options: He was murdered by the train driver.
He died of a heart attack in his signal box.
He was knocked down and killed by a train early in the morning.
questions.explanation: The men inform the narrator that the signalman was standing with his back to the train and was knocked down and killed that morning as it got light.

questions.question: Inference: The train driver shouted the exact same words and made the exact same arm movements as the "ghost." What does this mean about the ghost the signalman saw?
options: The ghost was actually trying to warn the signalman about his own upcoming death.
The train driver was playing a cruel trick on the signalman.
The signalman was the one driving the train.
questions.explanation: The ghost the signalman had been seeing recently was acting out the exact desperate actions the train driver would take right before the train hit the signalman, meaning the ghost was warning him of his own death.

questions.question: Purpose: Why did the author write a story where the main character cannot escape his fate, even with a warning?
options: To teach people how to work on a railway line.
To create a dark, mysterious tragedy about the fear of the unknown and the inability to change destiny.
To make the reader laugh at the signalman's mistakes.
questions.explanation: By showing that the warning was completely useless because it lacked specifics, the author creates a tragic, helpless mood where destiny cannot be avoided.

chapters.title: LIGEIA
chapters.passage:
I cannot remember how, when or where I met Ligeia. It was a long time ago and my memory is not good. But I think I met her first in a large, old city near the Rhine in Germany.

She told me that she came from an ancient family. But I never knew the family name of the woman who was my friend, my partner in my studies and finally my wife. Why did I never discover her family name? Perhaps because she did not want me to find out, but I cannot remember.

I remember one thing very well: Ligeia was tall and slim. Later, at the end, she became very thin. How can I describe her quiet, aristocratic movements, or the strange softness of her footsteps? If she came into my office, I only knew she was there when I heard her voice, or when she put her white hand on my shoulder.

She had a beautiful face, but it was not a classical kind of beauty. There was something strange about it. I have often tried to understand it: was it her pure white skin or her thick, black hair? I looked at her long, delicate nose many times. It was perfect! I looked at her sweet mouth. How soft and red it was! And when she smiled, her teeth were white. Then I looked into her eyes.

They were much bigger than normal eyes. Sometimes, when she was excited, they looked like a deer's eyes. They were black, with long black eyelashes and black eyebrows. But as I looked into them, I realised that they had a strange expression. I thought about it for many hours, sometimes all night. What was the expression in those eyes? I wanted to know. Many times I thought I almost had the answer, but then it was gone.

Ligeia was very determined. She was always calm and quiet, but her determination showed in her eyes. It shone like a terrible energy, and sometimes it frightened me.

Ligeia was very clever. She was excellent at Latin and Greek, and she knew many other languages perfectly; she never made a mistake. She was also a student of science and mathematics. When we were first married I often asked her for help with my studies, and we worked together. But after she died I was alone. Without her I was like a child in the dark.

When she first became ill, she did not come to help me as often as before. She lost weight and her skin became pale and transparent.

When I saw that she was dying, I felt desperate. Ligeia resisted death with all her energy - she was determined to live. I watched in agony as she fought for life.

I knew she loved me, but I only understood how much she loved me now that she was dying. She held my hands and said that she was devoted to me. I cannot talk about it now, but let me say that her love for me was part of her determination to live. On the night she died she suddenly got out of bed and cried, 'Oh God, must I die? Must I lose my fight with death? No, I can't die like this!'

But my dear Ligeia died. I was so sad I could not stay in the old city by the Rhine. For a few months I travelled around, then I bought an old abbey in an isolated part of England. This dark, sad place expressed my feelings of loneliness. But I decorated it with beautifully coloured curtains, carpets and ornaments. I said to myself, 'Perhaps the bright colours will make me feel happier.'

Unfortunately they did not. I began to drink too much. But I do not want to speak about that time of my life. I will only say that one day I married Lady Rowena Trevanion of Tremaine. My new wife had blonde hair and blue eyes. She was very different from my first wife, but how could I ever forget Ligeia?

I took Lady Rowena back to a room high up in the tower of the abbey, where we lived for the first month of our marriage. The room was very large, with an enormous window made of glass from Venice. The ceiling was high, like a church, and in the center there was a big gold chandelier. There were sofas from the East, and an Indian bed. On the walls were long tapestries, like carpets, with designs made of gold. The tapestries moved every time the wind blew.

My wife was afraid of me because I was often sad and depressed. She did not love me much and stayed away from me, but I preferred this. I always thought about Ligeia my beautiful, Ligeia, dead in the tomb. Sometimes in my dreams I called to her in the night. I imagined that perhaps my love for her could bring her back to me.

At the beginning of the second month Lady Rowena became ill. She did not sleep very well, and told me she could hear sounds and movements in the tower.

'You have a fever,' I said. 'You're imagining things.'

She got better, but then she went back to bed with a second illness, worse than the first. The doctors could not understand it. Again Rowena began to hear little sounds and movements in the bedroom, and they frightened her.

One night at the end of September she woke up suddenly. I was sitting on a sofa by her bed. She whispered to me that she could hear sounds and see movements, and there was a frightened expression on her thin face. But I saw and heard nothing.

'It's the wind,' I explained. 'You can see the tapestries moving in the wind.'

But her face was white with fear, and she nearly fainted. I remembered that there was some wine on the table on the other side of the room. As I walked under the light of the chandelier, a strange thing happened. I felt something invisible pass me, and on the carpet I saw a shadow, almost the shadow of a shadow. I decided to say nothing to Rowena.

I poured out a glass of wine and gave it to her. Then I sat on the sofa and watched her. After some moments I heard very quiet footsteps on the carpet, coming towards the bed. A second later, as Rowena was about to drink the wine, I saw - or perhaps I dreamed that I saw three or four large drops of a bright red liquid fall into the glass. Rowena did not see it; she drank the wine, and I said nothing because I thought it was only my imagination.

After this, Rowena's health got much worse, and on the third night she died. Her servants prepared her for the tomb, then covered her with a sheet. The next night I sat alone with her body in the bedroom. Strange forms and shadows moved around me. I looked nervously into the dark corners, at the moving tapestries, and I felt frightened.

Then I looked at the carpet under the chandelier. There was no shadow there, and I felt better. When I looked at Rowena on the bed, sad memories of Ligeia - the only woman I ever loved came back to me.

It was perhaps around midnight when I heard a sound. It was quiet but clear, and it woke me from my dreams. I thought it came from the bed. I listened in terror, but I did not hear it again. I looked carefully at Rowena for any sign of life. She was not moving, but I continued to look at her.

Minutes passed. Then I noticed a little colour in Rowena's face. My heart stopped in horror; I could not move. When I understood that Rowena was not dead, I tried to revive her. But soon the colour disappeared from her cheeks, her face looked like marble again and her lips were thin with the horrible expression of death. When her body was cold and rigid, I fell on to the sofa and dreamed about Ligeia.

An hour later I heard the same sound as before. I listened; yes, there it was again a sigh from the bed! I ran over and saw clearly that her lips were trembling. Then they opened, showing her bright teeth. I thought I was going mad. There was a pink colour on her cheeks and neck, her body was getting warm again and her heart was beating a little. Lady Rowena was alive!

I did everything I could to revive her. Then suddenly her colour disappeared, her heart stopped and her body became cold and rigid. I sat down and began to think about Ligeia again. Then again for the third time there was a sound from the bed. But why must I describe the horrors of that night? Again I tried to revive Rowena, and then a fourth time. Each time she seemed to fight with an invisible force; and each time her body changed. I cannot say how, but she looked different.

It was nearly dawn I when she moved again. I was sitting on the sofa, exhausted, but Rowena's body moved with more energy than before. Her colour returned, signs of life changed her face. Her eyes were closed, but she looked alive. Then she suddenly got out of bed and walked slowly to the centre of the room, like she was walking in her sleep.

I did not tremble; I did not move. I was as cold and still as stone, paralysed by what I saw. As I looked at her, my head filled with wild thoughts. Was Rowena really alive? Could I really see her blonde hair and blue eyes? Why wasn't I certain? I could not see her mouth very well, but her cheeks were like pink roses. Weren't they Rowena's cheeks? But wasn't she taller than before?

I was filled with a kind of madness. I ran to her, but she moved away. Then I saw her long hair moving in the wind - it was blacker than the black of midnight! And now slowly her eyes opened.

I shouted like a madman, 'These are the black eyes of my lost love - the eyes of Ligeia!'

questions.question: Main Idea: What is the main plot of this story?
options: A man tries to solve a medical mystery in a dark, isolated abbey in England.
A man's obsessive grief for his deceased, powerful first wife manifests in a terrifying, supernatural way through his second wife.
A man marries two women from very ancient, aristocratic German families.
questions.explanation: The plot follows the narrator's deep obsession with his first wife, Ligeia, whose powerful will to live eventually causes her to supernaturally take over the body of his second wife.

questions.question: Detail: According to the narrator, what was unique about Ligeia's intelligence?
options: She was an expert in modern technology.
She was completely uneducated but very creative.
She knew multiple languages perfectly, including Latin and Greek, and was a student of science and mathematics.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states she was excellent at Latin, Greek, many other languages, and was a student of science and mathematics.

questions.question: Inference: The narrator says Ligeia's eyes showed a determination that "shone like a terrible energy, and sometimes it frightened me." What does this suggest about Ligeia?
options: She possessed an incredibly powerful, almost unnatural force of will.
She was very angry and aggressive towards the narrator.
She was physically very weak from the beginning.
questions.explanation: Her determination is described as a "terrible energy" that frightened him, foreshadowing that her willpower is unnaturally strong.

questions.question: Detail: How does Ligeia react when she realizes she is going to die?
options: She accepts it peacefully and tells her husband to remarry.
She fights it with desperate energy, crying out, "Must I lose my fight with death? No, I can't die like this!"
She refuses to speak to her husband.
questions.explanation: The text says she resisted death with all her energy, crying out in agony that she couldn't die like this.

questions.question: Inference: Why did the narrator decorate his isolated English abbey with brightly colored curtains and carpets?
options: Because he was hosting a large party for his new wife.
He hoped the bright, cheerful decorations would cure his deep depression and loneliness over losing Ligeia.
Because Ligeia had told him to do it before she died.
questions.explanation: He states he decorated the dark abbey with bright colors, telling himself, "Perhaps the bright colours will make me feel happier."

questions.question: Detail: How is Lady Rowena physically different from Ligeia?
options: Rowena is tall with black hair, while Ligeia was short with red hair.
Rowena is described as having blonde hair and blue eyes, contrasting with Ligeia's black hair and dark eyes.
Rowena is much older than Ligeia was.

questions.question: Inference: Why was Lady Rowena afraid of the narrator?
options: Because he was often sad, depressed, and clearly still obsessed with his dead first wife.
Because he physically harmed her.
Because she knew he was secretly a doctor.
questions.explanation: The text says she was afraid because he was often sad and depressed, and he notes he preferred her staying away so he could think about Ligeia.

questions.question: Detail: When Lady Rowena is sick in the tower room, what does the narrator see fall into her glass of wine?
options: A poisonous spider.
Three or four large drops of a bright red liquid.
A piece of the gold chandelier.
questions.explanation: As Rowena is about to drink, the narrator sees "three or four large drops of a bright red liquid fall into the glass."

questions.question: Inference: The narrator sees a mysterious shadow, hears quiet footsteps, and watches drops of red liquid fall into Rowena's wine, but he says nothing. Why might he stay quiet?
options: He believes he is dreaming or that his grief and drinking are causing him to hallucinate.
He is the one poisoning her and doesn't want her to know.
He thinks Rowena's servants are playing a trick on her.
questions.explanation: Because of his fragile mental state and the strange environment, he dismisses the terrifying supernatural events, stating, "I thought it was only my imagination" or "perhaps I dreamed that I saw [it]."

questions.question: Detail: After Rowena dies, what does the narrator do the following night?
options: He leaves the abbey and returns to Germany.
He sits alone with her body in the large, dark bedroom, thinking sad memories of Ligeia.
He invites the doctors back to examine her.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states, "The next night I sat alone with her body in the bedroom... sad memories of Ligeia - the only woman I ever loved came back to me."

questions.question: Inference: When Rowena's body repeatedly shows signs of life and then dies again, the narrator says, "Each time she seemed to fight with an invisible force; and each time her body changed." What is the "invisible force"?
options: A medical condition the doctors failed to diagnose.
The spirit of Ligeia actively taking over Rowena's physical body.
The wind blowing through the tall tapestries.
questions.explanation: Based on Ligeia's established "determination to live" and the final reveal, the invisible force causing Rowena's body to change is Ligeia's spirit fighting to possess it.

questions.question: Text Structure: How does the author build suspense during the night Rowena's body lies in the bed?
options: By having Rowena wake up immediately and start screaming.
By repeating a cycle of the body showing brief signs of life, dying again, and physically changing slightly each time, drawing out the tension.
By describing the history of the abbey in great detail.
questions.explanation: The author creates agonizing suspense by having the body revive, then die, then revive again four separate times, with the narrator noting that "each time her body changed."

questions.question: Detail: When the body finally gets out of bed and walks to the center of the room, what makes the narrator start to question if it is actually Rowena?
options: She starts speaking in perfect Greek and Latin.
She is wearing Ligeia's clothes.
He notices she has grown taller than Rowena was.
questions.explanation: As the body stands in the room, his wild thoughts begin with questioning her height: "But wasn't she taller than before?"

questions.question: Inference: The narrator shouts, "These are the black eyes of my lost love - the eyes of Ligeia!" What is the final, horrifying realization?
options: Rowena was actually wearing a disguise the entire time.
Ligeia's powerful determination to live allowed her spirit to conquer death by resurrecting herself in Rowena's corpse.
The narrator realizes he has gone completely blind.
questions.explanation: The transformation is complete. Ligeia's black hair and black eyes have replaced Rowena's blonde hair and blue eyes, proving Ligeia's will defeated death.

questions.question: Purpose: Why does the author focus so heavily on Ligeia's incredible willpower and her desperate fight against death in Chapter One?
options: To establish the supernatural premise that her will was strong enough to overcome death itself in Chapter Two.
To explain why she was so good at mathematics.
To show that the doctors in Germany were very skilled.
questions.explanation: By establishing Ligeia's fierce, terrifying determination to live in the first chapter, the author makes the supernatural resurrection in the second chapter a logical payoff to her character trait.
